titel: Saving and withdrawing over the life cycle
kurz: Why the same equity allocation can be right at 35 and dangerous at 68, and what role future labour income and the direction of cash flows play in this.

bloecke.md: The appropriate split of wealth between equities and low-risk investments changes over the course of a lifetime. It depends on two quantities that change in a predictable way: the stock of future labour income and the direction of cash flows. Age as such is not the reason. As long as money flows into the portfolio, new units are bought more cheaply after a slump. As soon as money flows out, the same slump leads to a loss of substance that is never made up, because the units sold do not take part in the recovery.

## Human capital as a bond-like position

At 30, an employee with a permanent contract owns a second asset alongside the portfolio: the present value of all future net income. With a secure income, this [[Human capital|human capital]] behaves like a very long-dated bond whose interest develops roughly in line with inflation. The cash flow from it is largely independent of share prices. If you include this position, total wealth is already extremely bond-heavy. The small financial part of it can then be invested entirely in equities without the risk of total wealth becoming too high.

A declining equity allocation can therefore only be justified in a theoretically clean way by shrinking human capital. With each working year, the implicit bond gets smaller, and the portfolio has to take on a growing share of the bond position itself.

bloecke.formel: Human capital = sum over t of E_t / (1 + r)^t
bloecke.erklaerung: Present value of future net income up to the start of the pension. The calculation uses real income and a real discount rate so that the result is stated in today's purchasing power.

bloecke.beispiel: With real net income of €42,000 a year, 37 years until the pension starts at 67 and a discount rate of 2%, the present value at age 30 is around €1.11 million.

bloecke.md: The following illustrative calculation assumes real net income of €42,000 up to age 67, a real discount rate of 2%, real savings of €6,000 a year, a real portfolio return of 5% and a starting portfolio of €20,000 at age 30. The aim is equity risk that amounts to a constant 40% of total wealth over the entire lifetime.

bloecke.md: The derivation does not apply if income is equity-like. This affects, for example, self-employed people whose orders depend on the economic cycle, employees in cyclical industries and salespeople with a high bonus component. Their human capital loses value in the same phases in which share prices fall. For them, a lower equity allocation in the portfolio is therefore right. The extreme case is employee shares or stock options of your own employer. Job and portfolio then depend on the same company, and in the worst case both are lost together.

bloecke.titel: The statutory pension in total wealth
bloecke.md: Economically, a pension entitlement is a lifelong payment linked to wage growth. It is thus also a bond-like position, one that continues after working life and merely changes its form. Pensioners who cover their ongoing fixed costs from the statutory pension and a company pension hardly need a low-risk portion in the portfolio, because they do not have to sell units in a crash. The pension is, however, taxed. For a pension starting in 2026, around 84% of the pension is taxable under Section 22 no. 1 sentence 3 letter a EStG (Income Tax Act). Since the Growth Opportunities Act (Wachstumschancengesetz), this share rises by only 0.5 percentage points for each new cohort of pensioners.

## Equity risk and investment horizon

High equity allocations at a young age are usually justified by the argument that good and bad years balance out over long periods. Siegel bases this view on mean reversion (the tendency of returns to revert to their long-term average) in the US data. Samuelson and Merton reach the opposite result with a formal model. With constant relative risk aversion and returns that are independent of each other, the result is an optimal equity allocation in which the investment horizon does not appear.

bloecke.erklaerung: Optimal equity share according to Merton (1969). Age, remaining time horizon and level of wealth do not appear in the formula. Samuelson's objection to time diversification is based on this.

bloecke.md:
Bodie framed the argument as a question about the price of protection. If equities were safer over long periods, an option that protects against a loss relative to the risk-free rate would have to become cheaper as its term lengthens. Its price, however, rises with the term.

The data partly support both sides. The probability of a loss falls with the horizon, but it does not reach zero. In the Fama/French data from 1926 to 2026, the market premium, that is, the equity return above the risk-free rate, was negative in 13.5% of all rolling ten-year windows. US equities returned minus 0.8% a year in real terms from 1966 to 1981, and the same from 2000 to 2012. In addition, the possible size of a loss in euros grows with every year of saving, because the portfolio grows. [[Time diversification]] therefore makes a good outcome more likely, but it does not make the investment safer. The sound reason for high equity allocations at a young age therefore remains human capital and not the length of the investment horizon.
With a lump-sum investment, only the geometric average return matters. With ongoing contributions or withdrawals, it also matters in which years good and bad returns occur.

## Sequence risk in the withdrawal phase

With a lump-sum investment without deposits or withdrawals, the order of returns plays no role, because the annual returns are multiplied together and the order of the factors does not change the product. With ongoing withdrawals, this no longer holds. If the market falls in the first years, units are sold at low prices, and these units are permanently missing in the later recovery. [[Sequence risk]] is thus the reverse of the cost-averaging effect.

bloecke.titel: Two withdrawal paths with the same 25 annual returns
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with a starting portfolio of €500,000, fully invested in the MSCI World (net, euros), and a withdrawal of €20,000 at the start of each year, increased by 2% annually. The x-axis counts the years of the withdrawal phase from 1 to 25. Blue shows the returns from 2001 to 2025 in historical order, gold the same returns in reverse. Both series have the same geometric average return of 6.26% p.a.

bloecke.md:
In the historical order, the loss years 2001 and 2002 fell in the period when the portfolio was still almost full. By the end of 2007, before the loss year 2008, it had already shrunk to around €291,000. At the end of 2021, €5,040 was left in it, and in 2022 it was used up. In total, €520,706 could be withdrawn; then the payments ended after 22 years.

In reverse order, €1,289,795 is in the portfolio after the same 25 years, and all withdrawals, totalling €640,606, were paid. The mean, dispersion and geometric return of the two return series are identical. The difference arises solely from the order.

For a savings plan, the order works the other way round. A savings plan of €6,000 a year over the same 25 years reaches €610,498 in the historical order, but only €253,681 in reverse order. Savers benefit from bad early years to the same extent that investors in the withdrawal phase suffer from them.

## Measures against sequence risk

Three measures are available, and they differ in how well they work.

With the **cash bucket**, two to three years' worth of withdrawals are held ready in low-risk form. In loss years, withdrawals come from this reserve instead of from selling units. The effect exists but is smaller than it appears. Economically, the cash bucket mostly corresponds to an equity allocation a few percentage points lower, combined with a rule that makes it easier to stay the course. If the reserve is topped up again after every good year, units are at least sold systematically after price rises.

A lower withdrawal rate is the most effective, if least spectacular, measure. Using US data from 1926 to 1995, the Trinity study found withdrawal rates of 3% to 4% to be largely sustainable over a period of 30 years. For horizons of 50 years or more and at high valuation levels, the reliable rate tends to fall to 3.25% to 3.5%. German taxes and costs are not included in these figures. The individual withdrawal strategies are covered in the chapter on retirement.

With **dynamic withdrawal**, a fixed percentage of the current balance is withdrawn each year instead of a fixed amount. Mathematically, the portfolio can then never be used up. The disadvantage is that income fluctuates with the portfolio value.

bloecke.titel: Withdrawal of 4% of the current balance, 2001 to 2025
bloecke.unter: The same return series and the same starting portfolio of €500,000 as above, but with a percentage withdrawal instead of a fixed one. The withdrawals are converted into 2001 purchasing power (HICP Germany). The portfolio ends at €822,809 in nominal terms. The withdrawal fell to €7,271 in 2009 and was below the starting value in all 24 years after 2001, and in nominal terms in the 18 years from 2002 to 2019.

bloecke.md: When fund units are sold, the units bought first are deemed to be sold first (Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG). Withdrawals therefore come from the oldest units, which usually contain the highest gains. As a result, the taxable portion of a withdrawal is highest at the start of retirement and falls later. The gain is subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) under Section 32d(1) EStG plus the solidarity surcharge, 26.375% in total. For equity funds, the tax is reduced by the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) under Section 20 InvStG (Investment Tax Act). The advance lump sums (Vorabpauschalen) assessed under Section 18 InvStG during the holding period are deducted in full from the capital gain (Section 19(1) InvStG). If taxable income in retirement is low, the most-favourable assessment (Günstigerprüfung) under Section 32d(6) EStG should be applied for. If the personal marginal tax rate is below 25%, the lower rate is applied.

Ayres and Nalebuff draw the most far-reaching conclusion from the human capital argument. By their calculation, young investors hold too few equities in absolute euro terms because their portfolio is small. The table above shows this as a mathematically required allocation of 2,265% at age 30. They propose investing with borrowed money at a young age, with leverage of at most 2:1, in order to spread equity risk more evenly over a lifetime.

There are weighty objections to the proposal. Margin calls force sales at market lows and thus destroy the intended spreading of risk over time. Loan interest rates for private investors are well above the risk-free rate. In Germany, there is no cheap loan that runs for decades and cannot be terminated by the lender. In addition, the backtests depend heavily on the US data set. A weaker version is less spectacular but defensible: consistently holding 100% equities at a young age, keeping the emergency fund out of the portfolio and paying off any outstanding consumer loan before making any investment.

mitnehmen: A declining equity allocation can only be justified by shrinking human capital and not by age as such; if you count this implicit bond, the total wealth of someone starting their career is already extremely bond-heavy.
With income that depends on the economic cycle, human capital is equity-like, and the equity allocation in the portfolio must then fall instead of rise.
Time diversification lowers the probability of loss but not the risk; the Merton formula for the optimal equity allocation does not contain the investment horizon.

With a lump-sum investment, the order of returns plays no role, but with ongoing withdrawals it is decisive; in the model, the same 25 annual returns led once to a portfolio used up after 22 years and once to remaining wealth of €1.29 million.
The main defence against sequence risk is a lower or flexible withdrawal rate; the cash bucket largely corresponds to a lower equity allocation with fixed rules.

begriffe.text: The present value of all future net income from work. With a secure income, it acts like a large bond position in total wealth and allows a higher equity allocation in the portfolio. With income that depends on the economic cycle, it behaves like equities and requires a lower equity allocation.

The change in the equity allocation planned over a lifetime (also written glidepath). In theory, it can be justified by shrinking human capital; age itself is not a reason. It therefore stays flat for a long time and only falls steeply in the last years of working life.

The risk that the order of returns determines the result. With ongoing withdrawals, bad early years damage the portfolio permanently, because units sold no longer take part in the recovery. With a lump-sum investment without cash flows, this risk does not exist.

The thesis that equities become safer with a longer investment horizon. The probability of loss does fall, but the possible size of a loss in euros rises. The horizon does not appear in the Merton formula for the optimal equity allocation.

Reserve of two to three years' withdrawals in the low-risk portion that is used in loss years instead of selling units. Economically, it mostly corresponds to a slightly lower equity allocation and is at the same time an effective rule against panic selling.
